results.name: digit_match_near_minus_far
results.description: Among targets sharing a final digit with at least one example, yes rate when the nearest example is within 10 minus yes rate when it is more than 30 away; observed above null means numerical proximity boosts digit-matched targets, which the magnitude-blind model cannot capture.
results.code:
# name: digit_match_near_minus_far
# description: Among targets sharing a final digit with at least one example, yes rate when the nearest example is within 10 minus yes rate when it is more than 30 away; observed above null means numerical proximity boosts digit-matched targets, which the magnitude-blind model cannot capture.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    parts = s.str.split(",", expand=True)
    X = parts.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(X)
    Xf = np.where(valid, X, -1000.0)
    dist = np.abs(Xf - t[:, None])
    dist = np.where(valid, dist, np.inf)
    mind = dist.min(axis=1)
    match = (valid & ((np.nan_to_num(X, nan=-1).astype(int) % 10) == (t % 10)[:, None])).any(axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    a = r[match & (mind <= 10)]
    b = r[match & (mind > 30)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: gcd_divisible_minus_not
results.description: On 2-4 example sets whose examples share a common divisor >=3, among targets with the same parity as every example, yes rate for targets divisible by that divisor minus those not divisible; observed above null means people infer common-factor/multiples rules that the final-digit model cannot represent.
results.code:
# name: gcd_divisible_minus_not
# description: On 2-4 example sets whose examples share a common divisor >=3, among targets with the same parity as every example, yes rate for targets divisible by that divisor minus those not divisible; observed above null means people infer common-factor/multiples rules that the final-digit model cannot represent.
def test_statistic(df):
    from functools import reduce
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = s.unique()
    gmap, pmap = {}, {}
    for u in uniq:
        xs = [int(v) for v in u.split(",")]
        gmap[u] = reduce(math.gcd, xs) if len(xs) > 1 else 0
        ps = set(x % 2 for x in xs)
        pmap[u] = ps.pop() if len(ps) == 1 else -1
    g = s.map(gmap).astype(int)
    p = s.map(pmap).astype(int)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    base = (g >= 3) & (p == (t % 2))
    div = (t % g.clip(lower=1)) == 0
    a = df.loc[base & div, "rating"]
    b = df.loc[base & ~div, "rating"]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: all_even_minus_all_odd_sets
results.description: Yes rate on sets whose examples are all even minus yes rate on sets whose examples are all odd (any target); observed below null means people generalize more narrowly from even sets (e.g. inferring multiples rules) than the parity-symmetric digit model predicts, above means more broadly.

results.name: set_size_u_shape
results.description: Mean yes rate on 1- and 4-example sets minus mean yes rate on 2- and 3-example sets; observed above null means generalization breadth depends non-monotonically on set size (broader for 1 and 4 examples) in a way the digit-similarity model, which has no set-size term, under-produces.

results.name: recency_digit_match
results.description: On 2-4 example sets, yes rate for targets sharing a final digit with the last-shown example but not the first, minus yes rate for targets sharing it with the first but not the last; observed above null means a recency (order) effect that the order-blind average-similarity model cannot produce, below means primacy.
results.code:
# name: recency_digit_match
# description: On 2-4 example sets, yes rate for targets sharing a final digit with the last-shown example but not the first, minus yes rate for targets sharing it with the first but not the last; observed above null means a recency (order) effect that the order-blind average-similarity model cannot produce, below means primacy.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    n = s.str.count(",") + 1
    first = s.str.split(",").str[0].astype(int)
    last = s.str.split(",").str[-1].astype(int)
    t = df["target"].astype(int) % 10
    mf = (first % 10) == t
    ml = (last % 10) == t
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    a = r[(n > 1) & ml & ~mf]
    b = r[(n > 1) & mf & ~ml]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: small_target_minus_rest
results.description: Yes rate for targets <= 20 minus yes rate for targets > 20 (all sets); observed below null means people reject small targets more than the magnitude-blind digit model predicts (a target-magnitude bias the model lacks), above means they favour them.

results.name: round_target_no_digit_match
results.description: Among targets sharing no final digit with any example, yes rate for targets that are multiples of 5 minus other targets; observed above null means people favour round numbers (a salience/roundness prior) that the final-digit model gives no credit to, below means they disfavour them.
results.code:
# name: round_target_no_digit_match
# description: Among targets sharing no final digit with any example, yes rate for targets that are multiples of 5 minus other targets; observed above null means people favour round numbers (a salience/roundness prior) that the final-digit model gives no credit to, below means they disfavour them.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    parts = s.str.split(",", expand=True)
    X = parts.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(X)
    Xi = np.nan_to_num(X, nan=-1).astype(int)
    match = (valid & ((Xi % 10) == (t % 10)[:, None])).any(axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    round5 = (t % 5) == 0
    a = r[~match & round5]
    b = r[~match & ~round5]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: singleton_same_digit_yes
results.description: Yes rate on 1-example sets for targets ending in the example's final digit (target != example); observed below null means the model over-generalizes from a single example's last digit (single-example digit matches are weaker than on multi-example sets), above means people endorse them even more.
results.code:
# name: singleton_same_digit_yes
# description: Yes rate on 1-example sets for targets ending in the example's final digit (target != example); observed below null means the model over-generalizes from a single example's last digit (single-example digit matches are weaker than on multi-example sets), above means people endorse them even more.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    n = s.str.count(",") + 1
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    m = n == 1
    x = pd.to_numeric(s.where(m, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).astype(int)
    sel = m & ((x % 10) == (t % 10)) & (x != t)
    if sel.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df.loc[sel, "rating"].mean())
